\(\displaystyle V^\top = \begin{bmatrix}-0.707107 & -0.707107 \\ -0.707107 & 0.707107\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 2)\)


\(\displaystyle U^\top y = \begin{bmatrix}-5098.02 \\ 452.36\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)\)


\(\displaystyle S^{-1}U^\top y = \begin{bmatrix}-3645.21 \\ 2155.3\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)\)


\(\displaystyle VS^{-1}U^\top y = \begin{bmatrix}1053.53 \\ 4101.58\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)\)


\(\displaystyle \hat\beta=D^{-1}VS^{-1}U^\top y = \begin{bmatrix}372.479 \\ 21.4797\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)\)


Check those geometric claims using the actual matrices:

show_matrix(r"U^\top U", U.T @ U)
show_matrix(r"V^\top V", Vt @ Vt.T)
show_matrix(r"Av_1", A @ Vt.T[:, 0])
show_matrix(r"s_1u_1", singular_values[0] * U[:, 0])
np.testing.assert_allclose(U.T @ U, np.eye(p), atol=1e-14)
np.testing.assert_allclose(Vt @ Vt.T, np.eye(p), atol=1e-14)
np.testing.assert_allclose(A @ Vt.T[:, 0], singular_values[0] * U[:, 0], atol=1e-14)

\(\displaystyle U^\top U = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1.40929e-17 \\ 1.40929e-17 & 1\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 2)\)


\(\displaystyle V^\top V = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 2)\)


\(\displaystyle Av_1 = \begin{bmatrix}-0.525509 \\ -0.462557 \\ -0.495884 \\ -0.431821 \\ -0.419231 \\ -0.592164 \\ -0.387014 \\ -0.597719\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)\)


\(\displaystyle s_1u_1 = \begin{bmatrix}-0.525509 \\ -0.462557 \\ -0.495884 \\ -0.431821 \\ -0.419231 \\ -0.592164 \\ -0.387014 \\ -0.597719\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)\)




Derive the least-squares solution from the decomposition
First project the outcomes onto the columns of \(U\):
\[c=U^\top y,\qquad y_\parallel=Uc,\qquad
y_\perp=y-Uc.\]
Each \(c_j=u_j^\top y\) is a dot product measuring how much of \(y\) lies along direction \(u_j\). \(y_\parallel\) lies in the fitted plane, while \(y_\perp\) is perpendicular to it. The model can fit the first part; no choice of coefficients can reproduce the second part. This is a geometric decomposition of the observed sample, not recovery of the true simulation errors.
Write \(z=V^\top\theta\). Because the two residual components are perpendicular, the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[\|y-A\theta\|^2
=\|c-Sz\|^2+\|y_\perp\|^2.\]
The second term cannot change as we vary coefficients. The first term is minimized at zero by setting \(z_j=c_j/s_j\). Thus
\[\hat z=S^{-1}U^\top y,\qquad
\hat\theta=V\hat z,\qquad
\hat\beta=D^{-1}\hat\theta.\]
This explains the solution formula rather than just prescribing a sequence of matrix multiplications. It also gives \(\hat y=UU^\top y\) and \(r=y-UU^\top y\). \(UU^\top\) is a projection matrix, not the \(8\times8\) identity: it preserves vectors in the fitted plane and removes perpendicular components. There are two fitted directions and six residual directions, which is where \(n-p=8-2=6\) comes from.

coordinates = U.T @ y
projected_y = U @ coordinates
perpendicular_y = y - projected_y
show_matrix(r"c=U^\top y", coordinates)
show_matrix(r"y_\parallel=Uc", projected_y)
show_matrix(r"y_\perp=y-Uc", perpendicular_y)
show_matrix(r"U^\top y_\perp", U.T @ perpendicular_y)
np.testing.assert_allclose(projected_y, X @ beta, atol=1e-10)
np.testing.assert_allclose(U.T @ perpendicular_y, np.zeros(p), atol=1e-10)

\(\displaystyle c=U^\top y = \begin{bmatrix}-5098.02 \\ 452.36\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)\)


\(\displaystyle y_\parallel=Uc = \begin{bmatrix}1970.57 \\ 1605.41 \\ 1798.73 \\ 1427.13 \\ 1354.1 \\ 2357.21 \\ 1167.23 \\ 2389.42\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)\)


\(\displaystyle y_\perp=y-Uc = \begin{bmatrix}-91.32 \\ 199.615 \\ 223.558 \\ -159.283 \\ 155.138 \\ -117.105 \\ -207.718 \\ -2.88465\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)\)


\(\displaystyle U^\top y_\perp = \begin{bmatrix}8.19167e-13 \\ -2.69876e-14\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 1)\)


Reading the final product from right to left: \(U^\top y\) expresses the outcome in the left singular-vector directions; \(S^{-1}\) divides by the singular values; \(V\) converts back to scaled coefficient coordinates; \(D^{-1}\) restores the original predictor units. Each intermediate coefficient vector is \(2\times1\). The signs of corresponding singular vectors can differ across software while giving the same reconstructed matrix and coefficients.

for j in range(p):
    show_dot(rf"(U^\top y)_{{{j+1}}}", U[:, j], y)
scaled_coordinates = (U.T @ y) / singular_values
for j in range(p):
    show_dot(rf"(VS^{-1}U^\top y)_{{{j+1}}}", Vt.T[j], scaled_coordinates)

\(\displaystyle (U^\top y)_{1} = (-0.37575198)\cdot(1879.25) + (-0.33073952)\cdot(1805.03) + \cdots + (-0.42738393)\cdot(2386.54)\approx -5098.0192\)


\(\displaystyle (U^\top y)_{2} = (0.12153867)\cdot(1879.25) + (-0.17840147)\cdot(1805.03) + \cdots + (0.46558765)\cdot(2386.54)\approx 452.35992\)


\(\displaystyle (VS^-1U^\top y)_{1} = (-0.70710678)\cdot(-3645.2111) + (-0.70710678)\cdot(2155.2969)\approx 1053.5284\)


\(\displaystyle (VS^-1U^\top y)_{2} = (-0.70710678)\cdot(-3645.2111) + (0.70710678)\cdot(2155.2969)\approx 4101.5785\)


\(S^{-1}\) and \(D^{-1}\) are diagonal, so multiplying by them simply divides each coordinate by its corresponding singular value or column scale.


Why small singular values matter
If \(s_j=0\), then \(Av_j=0\): moving the coefficients along that nonzero direction does not change any fitted outcome. The data cannot distinguish those coefficient choices. For example, adding a second copy of area lets one area coefficient increase while the other decreases by the same amount. Only their sum matters.
If \(s_j\) is small but positive, division by \(s_j\) amplifies changes in the outcome coordinates. The design is identifiable but coefficients can be sensitive to noise. The condition number \(\kappa(A)=s_{\max}/s_{\min}\) measures that sensitivity in the scaled coordinates. Strongly correlated predictors often produce small singular values; full rank alone does not guarantee precise estimates.

print("Condition number of scaled design:", singular_values[0] / singular_values[-1])
duplicated = np.column_stack([X, X[:, 1]])
duplicated_scaled = duplicated / np.linalg.norm(duplicated, axis=0)
duplicate_singular_values = np.linalg.svd(duplicated_scaled, compute_uv=False)
duplicate_threshold = (np.finfo(float).eps * max(duplicated.shape)
                       * duplicate_singular_values[0])
show_matrix(r"\text{singular values with duplicated area}", duplicate_singular_values)
print("Smallest value:", duplicate_singular_values[-1])
print("Numerical rank threshold:", duplicate_threshold)
assert duplicate_singular_values[-1] <= duplicate_threshold

Condition number of scaled design: 6.663490322078895


\(\displaystyle \text{singular values with duplicated area} = \begin{bmatrix}1.71506 \\ 0.242043 \\ 1.62057e-17\end{bmatrix}\quad(3\times 1)\)


Smallest value: 1.620565314202345e-17
Numerical rank threshold: 3.0465504588638278e-15


In floating-point arithmetic, an exact zero may appear as a tiny positive number. Our threshold treats such directions as numerically rank deficient and rejects the fit with a clear error. It does not silently discard a predictor or divide by a nearly zero value.
Finally, \(A^\top A=VS^2V^\top\), so forming the normal-equation matrix squares the singular values and its condition number is \(\kappa(A)^2\). This can lose accuracy before a solve even begins. SVD works with \(A\) directly and exposes its rank. It avoids that extra numerical damage; it cannot make redundant predictors identifiable or make noisy data informative.

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
text:
3. Residuals and degrees of freedom
Full rank means we estimate \(p\) coefficients, leaving \(n-p\) independent residual directions. The unbiased variance estimate is
\[s^2=\frac{RSS}{n-p},\qquad s=\sqrt{s^2}.\]
The result fields are fitted, residuals, rss, df_residual, residual_variance, and sigma. We preserve actual floating-point residuals; we do not round nearly perfect fits to zero.

fitted = X @ beta
residuals = y - fitted
rss = residuals @ residuals
df = n - p
variance = rss / df
sigma = np.sqrt(variance)

print(f"RSS={rss:.8f}; residual df={df}; variance={variance:.8f}; sigma={sigma:.8f}")

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
text:
4. Covariance, standard errors and t-tests
Under independent errors with constant variance,
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=s^2(X^\top X)^{-1}
=s^2D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1}.\]
The code computes the latter expression, without forming \(X^\top X\). Standard errors are the square roots of the diagonal. Under Gaussian errors, \((\hat\beta_j-\beta_j)/SE_j\) has a Student t distribution with \(n-p\) degrees of freedom. For \(H_0:\beta_j=0\), the statistic is \(t_j=\hat\beta_j/SE_j\), the two-sided p-value is \(2P(T\ge |t_j|)\), and the 95% interval is \(\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,n-p}SE_j\).
Use the survival function for upper tails to avoid subtracting a CDF close to one. These are conventional homoskedastic standard errors, not robust estimates.
For the fixed 95% interval, Rust finds the critical value by bisection on \(P(T>t)=0.025\). Large-sample checks found that statrs’ inverse-beta quantile lost precision at high residual degrees of freedom. Solving on the survival function preserves agreement with R; this notebook independently uses SciPy’s t.ppf. See the large-data report and the focused Rust critical-value test for the regression evidence.

scaled_inverse = (Vt.T / singular_values) @ (Vt / singular_values[:, None])
covariance = variance * scaled_inverse / scales[:, None] / scales[None, :]
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance))
t_statistics = beta / se
p_values = 2 * t.sf(np.abs(t_statistics), df)
critical = t.ppf(0.975, df)
conf_int = np.column_stack([beta - critical * se, beta + critical * se])
display(pd.DataFrame(covariance, index=["intercept", "area_m2"], columns=["intercept", "area_m2"]))
display(pd.DataFrame({"coefficient": beta, "SE": se, "t": t_statistics, "p": p_values,

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
text:
5. R-squared and the intercept convention
With a column of exact ones, use \(TSS=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\) and \(R^2=1-RSS/TSS\). Adjusted R-squared is \(1-(1-R^2)(n-1)/(n-p)\).
Without an intercept, use uncentered \(TSS=\sum_i y_i^2\) and adjusted R-squared \(1-(1-R^2)n/(n-p)\), matching R’s no-intercept convention. Do not compare centered and uncentered R-squared as if they used the same baseline.

has_intercept = bool(np.any(np.all(X == 1, axis=0)))
tss = np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2) if has_intercept else y @ y
r_squared = 1 - rss / tss
adj_r_squared = 1 - (1 - r_squared) * (n - int(has_intercept)) / df
print(f"R²={r_squared:.9f}; adjusted R²={adj_r_squared:.9f}")

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
section: 6. Gaussian likelihood explains the same estimator
text:
6. Gaussian likelihood explains the same estimator
For independent \(y_i\sim N(x_i^\top\beta,\sigma^2)\), multiply the normal densities and take logs:
\[\ell(\beta,\sigma^2)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{RSS(\beta)}{2\sigma^2}.\]
At fixed positive variance, maximizing this expression minimizes RSS, so it gives the same OLS coefficients. Differentiate with respect to \(v=\sigma^2\):
\[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v}=-\frac{n}{2v}+\frac{RSS}{2v^2}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\hat v_{ML}=RSS/n.\]
This ML variance differs from \(RSS/(n-p)\) used for standard errors. At the estimates,
\[\ell(\hat\beta,\hat v_{ML})=-\frac n2[\log(2\pi)+\log(RSS/n)+1].\]

ml_variance = rss / n
log_likelihood = -n / 2 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.log(ml_variance) + 1)
def log_likelihood_at(candidate, v):
    return -n / 2 * np.log(2 * np.pi * v) - rss_at(candidate) / (2 * v)
print(f"ML variance={ml_variance:.8f}; inference variance={variance:.8f}")
print(f"Log-likelihood={log_likelihood:.9f}")
assert log_likelihood_at(beta, ml_variance) > log_likelihood_at(beta + [0, 0.1], ml_variance)
assert log_likelihood_at(beta, ml_variance) > log_likelihood_at(beta, 2 * ml_variance)

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
section: 8. Missing data, singularity and perfect fits
text:
8. Missing data, singularity and perfect fits
The PHP call drops a whole row if any supplied predictor or its outcome is null or NAN, warns once on a successful fit, and reports original row positions. It applies all formulas above to the retained sample: \(n\) and \(n-p\) change. Use missing: 'raise' to reject missingness. Infinity, malformed values and rank failure remain errors. See missing-data contract.
Listwise deletion changes the estimation sample; it is not imputation and does not guarantee unbiased results when missingness is related to the outcome or predictors. Document why data are missing and which observations were retained.
At exact zero RSS, standard errors are zero and the Gaussian log-likelihood has an infinite limit as variance approaches zero. A zero coefficient divided by a zero standard error is undefined (NaN); a nonzero coefficient gives infinite t and zero p. If TSS is also zero, R-squared is undefined. Decomposition roundoff can leave small residuals in mathematically perfect fits; unstable t-statistics and likelihoods should not be compared tightly across algorithms.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
We observe simulated students, with study hours, a practice score and a binary pass/fail outcome. The column of ones estimates an intercept. R seed 20261013 generates 120 students: hours are uniform between 1 and 12, scores are clipped to 20–95 from 45 + 3 × hours + normal noise with standard deviation 8. Both are rounded to two decimals.
The underlying simulation is a latent normal threshold model:
\[z_i^*=-1.9+0.13\,\mathrm{hours}_i+0.011\,\mathrm{score}_i+\epsilon_i,
\quad \epsilon_i\sim N(0,1),\quad y_i=\mathbf{1}\{z_i^*>0\}.\]
With \(\eta_i=x_i^\top\beta\), symmetry of the standard normal gives \(P(y_i=1)=P(\epsilon_i>-\eta_i)=\Phi(\eta_i)\). The latent value is a model construction: only the resulting 0 or 1 is supplied to the estimator. Fixing the latent variance to one identifies the coefficient scale; there is no sigma to estimate.
The normal CDF \(\Phi(a)\) is the area under a standard-normal density to the left of \(a\). The density is \(\phi(a)=e^{-a^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\), and \(\Phi'(a)=\phi(a)\). Unlike a logit coefficient, \(e^{\beta_j}\) is not a constant odds multiplier. The local probability slope is \(\phi(\eta_i)\beta_j\), so it varies by observation.
The hand-worked iteration below starts from zero coefficients so the first weights and dot products are easy to inspect. phit also starts from zero, except for extreme inputs with a ones column, where it uses a finite marginal intercept start. Starting values change the iteration path, not the likelihood or the converged estimates.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
2. Likelihood and derivatives
For independent Bernoulli outcomes the log-likelihood is
\[\ell(\beta)=\sum_i[y_i\log\Phi(\eta_i)+(1-y_i)\log\Phi(-\eta_i)].\]
The complement is written \(\Phi(-\eta)\) to avoid subtracting a CDF rounded to one. Taking a derivative with respect to \(\eta_i\) gives
\[s_i=\phi(\eta_i)\frac{y_i-\pi_i}{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)},\qquad
\pi_i=\Phi(\eta_i),\qquad g=X^\top s.\]
For a success this is \(\phi/\Phi(\eta)\); for a failure it is \(-\phi/\Phi(-\eta)\). These ratios are evaluated from log density minus log tail probability. Rust uses erfc for ordinary tails and a normal Mills-ratio continued fraction beyond -8, preserving finite log-likelihoods even when the CDF underflows.
Expected negative curvature, or Fisher information, is
\[I=X^\top W X,\qquad
w_i=\frac{\phi(\eta_i)^2}{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)}.\]
One way to see this is to square \(s_i\) and take its expectation: \(E[(y_i-\pi_i)^2]=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\), leaving the expression above. Unlike canonical logistic regression, observed curvature and expected information need not agree at a finite probit sample. We use Fisher scoring and its covariance, matching R glm and statsmodels GLM; a discrete-model probit fit’s observed-Hessian covariance can differ without either calculation being erroneous.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
3. Scoring, weighted matrices and SVD
Fisher scoring solves \(I\Delta\beta=g\) and updates coefficients. For probit this is not Newton’s method, because expected information differs from the observed negative Hessian (section 2). To avoid forming and inverting the cross-product for fitting, define column scales \(D\), \(A=XD^{-1}\) and \(\theta=D\beta\). Solve
\[B\Delta\theta\approx q,\quad B=W^{1/2}A,\quad q=W^{-1/2}s,
\qquad B=USV^\top,\quad \Delta\theta=VS^{-1}U^\top q.\]
The weighted least-squares normal equations are \(A^\top W A\Delta\theta=A^\top s\). This is the same update in scaled coordinates, with \(\Delta\beta=D^{-1}\Delta\theta\). We display cross-products to understand them; the production solve uses weighted SVD. See the OLS SVD explanation.
Weights and scores change each iteration: this is IRLS. The full increment can overshoot, so a decreasing-likelihood step is halved, at most 30 times. Both a small full coefficient increment and a small likelihood change are required. A tiny damped step alone does not establish convergence; the limit is 100 updates.

def values(eta):
    log_density = -0.5*eta**2-0.5*np.log(2*np.pi)
    probability = ndtr(eta)
    root = np.exp(log_density-0.5*(log_ndtr(eta)+log_ndtr(-eta)))
    score = np.where(y == 1, np.exp(log_density-log_ndtr(eta)), -np.exp(log_density-log_ndtr(-eta)))
    return probability,root,score

def log_likelihood(eta):
    return np.where(y == 1,log_ndtr(eta),log_ndtr(-eta)).sum()

scales = np.linalg.norm(X,axis=0)
A = X/scales
theta = np.zeros(p)
history=[]
for iteration in range(1,101):
    eta=A@theta
    fitted,root,score=values(eta)
    B=root[:,None]*A
    q=score/root
    U,singular,Vt=np.linalg.svd(B,full_matrices=False)
    assert np.all(singular > np.finfo(float).eps*max(n,p)*singular[0])
    step=Vt.T@((U.T@q)/singular)
    old_ll=log_likelihood(eta)
    fraction=1.0
    for _ in range(31):
        candidate=theta+fraction*step
        new_ll=log_likelihood(A@candidate)
        if np.isfinite(new_ll) and new_ll >= old_ll-16*np.finfo(float).eps*(1+abs(old_ll)): break
        fraction/=2
    else: raise RuntimeError("No improving step")
    if iteration==1:
        show_matrix(r"\beta^{(0)}",theta/scales)
        show_matrix(r"s^{(0)}",score)
        show_matrix(r"W^{(0)}_{1:5,1:5}\text{ (top-left block)}",np.diag(root[:5]**2))
        show_matrix(r"g^{(0)}=X^\top s",X.T@score)
        show_matrix(r"I^{(0)}=X^\top W X",X.T@(root[:,None]**2*X))
        for j in range(p): show_dot(rf"g_{{{j+1}}}",X[:,j],score)
        show_dot(r"I_{2,3}",X[:,1],root**2*X[:,2])
        show_matrix("B",B)
        show_matrix("q",q)
        show_matrix(r"U^\top q",U.T@q)
        show_matrix(r"\Delta\beta",step/scales)

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
4. Covariance and Wald inference
Evaluate information at the final coefficients, then compute
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=I(\hat\beta)^{-1},\quad
\operatorname{SE}_j=\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)_{jj}},\quad
z_j=\hat\beta_j/\operatorname{SE}_j.\]
The SVD supplies the covariance as \(D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1}\). Two-sided p-values use \(2P(Z\ge |z_j|)\) and 95% Wald limits use \(\hat\beta_j\pm1.959964\operatorname{SE}_j\). These are asymptotic normal tests, not OLS Student t tests. We do not multiply covariance by RSS/(n-p). R confint.default() supplies equivalent Wald intervals; ordinary GLM confint() uses profile likelihood instead.

_,singular,Vt=np.linalg.svd(root[:,None]*A,full_matrices=False)
covariance=((Vt.T/singular)@(Vt/singular[:,None]))/scales[:,None]/scales[None,:]
se=np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance))
z=beta/se
p_values=2*norm.sf(np.abs(z))
conf_int=np.column_stack([beta-norm.ppf(.975)*se,beta+norm.ppf(.975)*se])
show_matrix(r"\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)",covariance)
show_matrix(r"\hat\mu\text{ or }\hat\pi",fitted)
display(pd.DataFrame({"coefficient":beta,"SE":se,"z":z,"p":p_values,"95% lower":conf_int[:,0],"95% upper":conf_int[:,1]},index=["intercept",*observations.columns[:2]]))

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
5. Likelihood, deviance and AIC
For individual binary outcomes the saturated likelihood is zero, giving \(D=-2\ell(\hat\beta)\). The intercept-only null probability is the observed success proportion. Without a ones column, the null baseline is 0.5. Neither a latent variance nor an OLS residual variance is estimated. A probit coefficient is on the latent normal scale: multiplying it by a normal density converts it to a local probability slope, not an odds ratio.
AIC is \(2p-2\ell(\hat\beta)\); residual degrees of freedom are \(n-p\), without an estimated dispersion parameter. Predictions are probabilities, and residuals are observed minus fitted. These vectors follow retained input row order.

ll=log_likelihood(eta)
null_ll=np.sum(y*np.log(y.mean())+(1-y)*np.log1p(-y.mean()))
model_deviance=-2*ll
null_deviance=-2*null_ll
print("First local probability slope for predictor 1:",norm.pdf(eta[0])*beta[1])
calculated=dict(coefficients=beta,covariance=covariance,std_errors=se,z_statistics=z,p_values=p_values,
                conf_int=conf_int,fitted=fitted,residuals=y-fitted,log_likelihood=ll,
                deviance=model_deviance,null_deviance=null_deviance,aic=2*p-2*ll,df_residual=n-p)
for key,value in calculated.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value,case["expected"][key],atol=1e-9,rtol=1e-7,err_msg=key)
print({key:calculated[key] for key in ["log_likelihood","deviance","null_deviance","aic","df_residual"]})
print("Every statistical field agrees with the saved R fixture.")

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
6. Assumptions, failure modes and experiments
Both observed classes must remain after missing-row deletion. Complete or quasi separation can make a finite MLE nonexistent; encountered separating directions are rejected, as are singular information and iteration exhaustion. This certificate check is not exhaustive separation detection. Near separation can produce poor Wald inference even for a converged fit. Try replacing passed by study_hours > 6: what would happen to the latent coefficient as the probabilities approach the labels?
For both methods the retained design must have n > p and full numerical rank. Missing null/NAN rows are dropped with a warning unless missing: ‘raise’. No partial unconverged result is returned. See the contract and the executed three-way comparison.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
Rust connections
fit_probit owns its input vectors and converts them to nalgebra matrices. Borrowed matrix operands remain available for later iterations; iterators construct weights and score residuals. A dedicated loop performs this estimator’s updates. Result and ? propagate validation/numerical failures. The returned struct holds numeric fields; the PHP binding converts those fields into an associative array and adds warning/sample metadata. No generic optimizer or family hierarchy is added. See Rust learning notes and crates/stats-core/src/probit.rs.
Reference documentation: R glm, R families, statsmodels GLM.

title: R compatibility: target, coverage and remaining work
text:
phit aims to give the same statistical results as R and lme4 for the same data and model. This page lists what phit reproduces, where its results or conventions differ, and what it does not support. Agreement is established on the tested cases listed under Evidence and tolerances, not for every possible input. Full R/lme4 compatibility is a goal, not a claim about the current release.
Base R’s stats package supplies lm() and glm(). lme4 is a separate R package.

title: R compatibility: target, coverage and remaining work
text:
Differences from R
These are the differences in results and inference. Model formulas lists the differences in formula handling.

GLM covariance. phit reports the inverse information at the final coefficients. See GLM covariance.
glmer Laplace modes. phit solves each conditional mode to convergence. lme4’s default tolPwrss stops earlier. See glmer conditional modes.
Mixed-model inference. phit reports Wald z tests and p-values for fixed effects. lme4’s Gaussian summary reports t values without p-values. phit has no degrees-of-freedom correction (Satterthwaite or Kenward–Roger).
Group and term order. Groups follow first appearance after deletion, and random terms keep formula order. lme4 sorts levels and orders terms by their number of levels. Estimates do not depend on the order.
Rank deficiency. An aliased fixed column raises code 1004. R reports NA coefficients.
Zero weights and zero-column designs are rejected. R accepts them.
Nonconvergence raises an exception. R can return a fit object with a warning.
Sparse versus dense computation. lme4 uses a sparse Cholesky factor for every design. phit splits single and nested grouping terms into independent blocks, but crossed terms use a dense summary limited to 512 random coefficients and 50,000,000 entries in the initial augmented matrix.
Random numbers. Seeded sampling uses local ChaCha20 state, so sequences differ from R’s generators.
Vector semantics. Distribution and descriptive functions do not implement R’s recycling, coercion, or vector names.


GLM covariance
GLM covariances in phit are the inverse Fisher information at the final coefficients. R’s vcov() and summary() for a glm use the working weights of the last IRLS iteration, which come from the coefficients one step before the final update. R’s coefficients are already at the maximum to many digits, but its covariance differs from the information at those coefficients by about the size of the last step. The difference does not come from the convergence tolerance, from Fisher versus observed information (equal for the canonical logit and log links), or from dispersion (fixed at one).
For am ~ wt + hp on mtcars:

The coefficients agree to 12 digits. R’s last step changed them by 3.4e-8 relative.
The variance of the wt coefficient is 9.41676694948 from vcov() and 9.41676794579 from phit, 1.1e-7 relative.
Recomputing the information in R at coef(fit), or refitting with start = coef(fit), gives 9.41676794579.

Near separation the last step is larger, and the two can differ by about 1e-4 relative. phit’s R fixtures restart glm() from its own solution until the coefficients stop changing.


glmer conditional modes
fit_mixed_logistic() evaluates the Laplace approximation with each group’s conditional mode solved to convergence. lme4’s glmer() finds the modes by penalized iteratively reweighted least squares (PIRLS) and stops at glmerControl(tolPwrss = 1e-7) by default, which perturbs its objective enough to move the estimates. Not supported
Each item below is outside the current parity claim.
Formulas

subset and na.exclude arguments. Rows are deleted listwise, as na.omit does; see Missing values.

Functions outside the supported transforms, such as ns(), bs(), scale(), and C(). They raise code 1007.

GLM families and links other than Gaussian identity, binomial logit and probit, and Poisson log.

Configurable confidence levels for coefficient intervals, profile and bootstrap intervals, and likelihood-ratio tests.
Residual diagnostics, leverage, and influence measures.
Model-object methods such as update(), anova(), and simulate().

Mixed models

Binomial random slopes or several random terms, and mixed Poisson, probit, or negative-binomial likelihoods. fit_mixed_logistic() supports one random intercept.
nlmer() and other nonlinear mixed models.
Sparse computation for crossed designs beyond the dense limits.
Native NLopt and PORT (nlminb) backends, the full lme4 optimizer controls, restart policies, gradient and Hessian convergence checks, and an allFit()-style audit.
Prediction standard errors and intervals, and simulation of new observations.
Fixed-effect degrees-of-freedom corrections, and intervals for variance components or random effects.

dist_{family}_rng(int $n, int $seed, ...parameters): array takes the family’s parameters and defaults.

n is in [0, 1,000,000], and seed is a nonnegative PHP integer.
Every call uses its own ChaCha20 state and does not touch PHP’s random state.
Results are packed lists of n finite floats, including discrete counts.
The same seed and parameters reproduce the same draws, and a longer request extends a shorter one, within the same build.
An empty request still validates its parameters.




Failure
Code




Negative n or seed
1001


n above 1,000,000
1007


Nonfinite parameters or generated samples
1003


PHP argument-conversion errors
0



Seeded sampling defines the inverse-CDF method, the uniform grid, and the limits of reproducibility across versions and platforms.



The ten descriptive functions are stat_mean, stat_var, stat_sd, stat_cov, stat_cor, stat_quantile (type 7), stat_quantile_array, stat_median, stat_weighted_mean, and stat_weighted_var.







Rule
Behavior




Missing values
missing: 'raise' by default (code 1001). missing: 'drop' deletes them, pairwise for aligned inputs


Infinity
Always raises 1003


Normalization
Variance, SD, and covariance default to the sample (n − 1) divisor


Weighted variance
Frequency weights by default; reliability and population options


Negative weights
Rejected before missing-value deletion


Constant input to stat_cor
Returns NAN


Other nonfinite arithmetic
Raises 1003, so overflow cannot appear as zero variance



These defaults differ from the model functions, which drop missing rows by default, and from the draw kernels below, which accept no missing values. They do not depend on the input’s shape.
The verification record and benchmarks cover accuracy and speed.

text:
Posterior-draw numerical kernels
Phit\draws_moments(
    array $draws,
    ?array $weights = null,
    string $normalization = 'population',
): array;
Phit\draws_covariance_map(
    array $sourceCovariance,
    array $targetCovariance,
): array;
Phit\draws_affine(
    array $draws,
    array $matrix,
    array $shift,
): array;
Shared rules.

Draw matrices have one row per draw and one column per parameter, with at least one of each. All matrices must be rectangular.
Only integers and floats are accepted. null, strings, and booleans raise 1001; NAN and INF raise 1003. weights itself may be null for uniform weights.
Keys are ignored, iteration order sets the row and parameter order, and results are packed lists.
Inputs are not modified. No rows are dropped and no intercept is added; there is no missing or intercept option.
Ragged or incompatible dimensions raise 1002, and nonfinite arithmetic raises 1003.









Function
Returns
Rules




draws_moments
['mean' => list<float>, 'covariance' => list<list<float>>]
Weights are finite, nonnegative, one per draw, with positive total, and are normalized to sum to one


draws_covariance_map
['matrix' => list<list<float>>, 'log_abs_det' => float]
Both covariances square, finite, symmetric, positive definite, of equal size


draws_affine
['draws' => list<list<float>>, 'log_abs_det' => float]
A square, invertible matrix and a shift of the parameter dimension



draws_moments. The mean is \(\sum_i w_i x_i\) and the population covariance \(\sum_i w_i(x_i-\mu)(x_i-\mu)^T\). 'unbiased' divides the covariance by \(1-\sum_i w_i^2\), so weights express reliability, not frequency counts.

Zero total weight, an unknown normalization, or an undefined unbiased normalization raises 1001.
Zero-weight rows are still validated.
One effective draw is valid for population moments and gives zero covariance.
A singular covariance is valid, including when there are fewer draws than parameters.

draws_covariance_map. Returns \(A=L_tL_s^{-1}\) from the Cholesky factors and a triangular solve, so \(A C_s A^T=C_t\) to floating-point precision. The map depends on the parameter order and is not unique.

Asymmetry beyond the documented tolerance raises 1001.
A failed positive-definite factorization or a numerically singular matrix raises 1005.
There is no ridge, jitter, or other regularization.

draws_affine. Each row becomes \(y_i=A x_i+b\), or \(Y=X A^T+b\) in row-oriented notation. The output keeps the row and column counts and the draw order. Negative determinants are allowed, and log_abs_det is \(\log|\det A|\). A singular or numerically singular map raises 1004.
Posterior-draw kernels gives the tolerances, formulas, and verification. Stan evaluation, PSIS, moment matching, and diagnostics belong to the consuming CmdStan package.

Both follow R’s C code (Brent_fmin and R_zeroin2) step by step, so they evaluate f at the same points and return the same doubles.
The default tol is R’s .Machine$double.eps^0.25.
f is any PHP callable that takes one float and returns an int or float. Any other return value raises 1001. An exception thrown by f propagates unchanged.
As in R, a nonfinite value during the search is replaced by the largest finite value, keeping the sign of -INF in uniroot. One E_WARNING reports the replacement.
uniroot needs f(lower) and f(upper) without NAN and with opposite signs.
When uniroot runs out of iterations, it raises an E_WARNING, sets iter to maxiter, and returns its last estimate.
R’s extendInt and check.conv options are not available.

tests/optimize.php compares 91 results with R 4.6.1 bit for bit, including the number of function evaluations. The cases cover smooth, flat, kinked, multimodal, and boundary minima, infinite values, roots at the endpoints, a step function, and a search that does not converge. dist_{family}_rng(int $n, int $seed, ...parameters): array. The parameters and defaults are those of the probability functions.

n is an integer in [0, 1000000]. Both n and seed are required.
seed is a nonnegative PHP integer, from 0 to PHP_INT_MAX (2^63 − 1 on the supported 64-bit platforms).
The result is a packed list<float> of exactly n finite values. Discrete counts are floats too.
Sampling is already a batch operation, so there is no scalar form and no _array suffix.

title: Seeded batch sampling
text:
Reproducibility and state

The same seed and parameters give the same result within the same build.
A shorter request returns the prefix of a longer one.
Calls do not share a stream, so one call never advances another.
PHP’s mt_srand() and other application RNG state are neither read nor changed.
There is no time-based seed, no OS entropy, no retained RNG object, and no hidden global state.
A seed selects the same uniform sequence for every family, so reusing a seed couples the results through their quantiles. Use different seeds for batches that should be independent.
Seeds are not designed to match R’s or NumPy’s generators.
Results can change between phit versions when a dependency or quantile algorithm changes. Bitwise agreement across library versions, compilers, or platform math libraries is not promised.

examples/rng.php checks repeatability and the prefix property.

title: Seeded batch sampling
Seeded batch sampling
text:
Errors







Condition
Exception code




Negative n or seed, a parameter outside its domain, a non-list prob, a negative weight, a zero weight sum, min > max, or size > n
1001


Nonfinite parameter, weight, weight sum, or bound; a sample beyond the binary64 range
1003


More than one million draws or rows, or a permutation n above one million
1007


Wrong PHP argument type
PHP runtime error (code 0)




Parameters are validated even when n is 0. A valid empty request returns [].
A sample beyond the binary64 range rejects the whole batch. No partial results, dropped samples, or infinities are returned. Very heavy tails or extreme scales can therefore fail with finite parameters.
The one-million limit bounds one allocation. Callers control the total workload.

title: Seeded batch sampling
text:
Implementation and reproducibility
Each output takes a 64-bit word from ChaCha20. rand’s Open01<f64> maps its upper 52 bits to a midpoint strictly inside (0, 1), and the family’s validated inverse CDF transforms it.

One uniform per sample, including point masses.
The open interval excludes infinite support endpoints. The smallest and largest representable tail probabilities are 2^-53 and 1 − 2^-53.
Inverse-CDF sampling keeps one numerical path for all 13 parameterizations, at some cost against family-specific samplers. The sampling benchmarks measure normal, beta, and Poisson batches.
The pinned rand_core seed_from_u64 expands the integer seed into the 256-bit ChaCha key with its documented PCG32 mapping.
Dependencies: rand 0.9.5 and rand_chacha 0.9.0, pinned in the lock file. Their MIT license notices are under third-party/. A change to either, or to a quantile algorithm, is reviewed as a reproducibility change.


Independent verification
tests/generate-rng-fixtures.py implements the ChaCha20 block function, the PCG seed expansion, and the Open01 mapping independently, without calling the extension or rand. tests/generate-rng-fixtures.R maps those uniforms through base R’s quantile functions.







Fixture content (tests/fixtures/rng-python-r.json)
Values




Exact uniforms at four seeds, including 0 and PHP_INT_MAX
384


Transformed values for all 13 parameterizations, three extra normal seeds, and five point masses
1,616


Total, in 25 cases
2,000




Rust checks all values, and PHP checks the 1,616 transformed values.
Uniform and discrete values match exactly. The continuous tolerance is 1e-15 + 1e-12 * abs(reference).
The uniform, categorical, and permutation samplers are checked against the documented maps applied to the fixture’s uniforms.
Both suites also check repeatability, prefixes, state isolation, domains and limits, nonfinite samples, and normal and Poisson moments. PHP checks parameter names, defaults, and strict argument types.

PHP=/path/to/php PHP_CONFIG=/path/to/php-config ./scripts/check
